title: The Red Float
picture: A wooden boat shed on a muddy estuary at low tide, with a faded red cork fishing float hanging on a nail above the open door.
motif: the red cork float above the shed door
character_want: To hand over the keys of her late grandfather's boat shed and leave before the tide comes in.
character_hidden_feeling: Guilt that she stopped answering his calls in the last year of his life.

sections.exposition: Ines dragged the last crate of rope across the shed and let it thump down by the door. The air smelled of tar and wet mud, and every board gave a little under her trainers. Above the doorway hung the red cork float her grandfather had repainted every spring, its paint now flaking like old nail varnish. She left it on its nail. The buyer was due at four, and the tide turned at five.
sections.inciting_incident: Clearing the workbench, she lifted a tarpaulin and found the answering machine he had always refused to replace. A red light blinked on its scratched lid. One message. The date on the little screen was the second of March, the week she had stopped picking up his calls.
sections.rising_action:
She reached for the play button, but tyres crunched on the track outside, and she pulled her hand back as if the plastic were hot. It was almost a relief. She yanked the plug from the wall and decided the machine would go in the skip with the broken lobster pots, unheard.

But the buyer, a man called Pryce, walked straight past the skip and lifted the machine out. "These old ones sell online," he said, turning it over. "Mind if I keep it?" The thought of a stranger hearing that voice made her snatch it back. She would take it with her, she told him, and sign quickly so he left.

She signed all three pages on the bonnet of his car. Pryce shook her hand and drove off, but by then the tide had crept over the low part of the track, brown and flat, cutting the shed off from the road. Her car sat on the far side of the water. Nothing was left to pack.
sections.climax: The machine sat on the empty bench. She found the socket by the door. Salt had crusted round its edges. The plug's prongs were bent, and she straightened them with her thumbnail. It went in on the second try. The red light came back. She could still pull the plug out again. She stood with one finger on the button for a long time. Water lapped at the bottom step. A gull walked along the roof, its feet clicking on the tin. She pressed down.
sections.falling_action: His voice came out thin and crackly. He was not angry. He wanted to know whether she would like the float red again this year or blue for a change, since she was the one who always used to choose. He said he would wait to hear from her. The tape clicked and stopped.
sections.resolution: Ines lifted the float off its nail. Flakes of red came away on her palm and stuck there. She carried it down to the water's edge and stood holding it while the tide rose over her trainers, cold through the canvas. Then she tucked it under her arm, the way he used to, and started wading towards the car.

rising_beats.beat_1: She reached for the play button, but tyres crunched on the track outside, and she pulled her hand back as if the plastic were hot. It was almost a relief. She yanked the plug from the wall and decided the machine would go in the skip with the broken lobster pots, unheard.
rising_beats.beat_2: But the buyer, a man called Pryce, walked straight past the skip and lifted the machine out. "These old ones sell online," he said, turning it over. "Mind if I keep it?" The thought of a stranger hearing that voice made her snatch it back. She would take it with her, she told him, and sign quickly so he left.
rising_beats.beat_3: She signed all three pages on the bonnet of his car. Pryce shook her hand and drove off, but by then the tide had crept over the low part of the track, brown and flat, cutting the shed off from the road. Her car sat on the far side of the water. Nothing was left to pack.

briefs.exposition: Open mid-task as Ines clears the shed, give one concrete sensory detail of the place, and plant the red float she chooses to leave behind.
briefs.inciting_incident: Break the routine of packing with one discovery: the unheard answering-machine message from the week she stopped answering.
briefs.rising_action: Three beats that each push her away from the message and fail: she bins the machine, the buyer tries to keep it, then the tide traps her with nothing left to do.
briefs.climax: Slow right down as Ines chooses to plug the machine in and press play, using small physical details of the socket, plug and button.
briefs.falling_action: Let the message play: the grandfather's ordinary, unangry question about the float, then silence.
briefs.resolution: Bring the float back so it now means his question and her answer; end on an action, not an explanation.

title: Eight Minutes Slow
picture: An empty laundrette at night: a row of round dryer doors, one hanging open, and a scratched wristwatch lying on the folding table.
motif: his father's wristwatch, which runs eight minutes slow
character_want: To close his aunt's laundrette without a single mistake so she keeps trusting him with the keys.
character_hidden_feeling: Fear that he is like his father, who went to prison for theft, and shame about how badly he needs money.

sections.exposition: "Ten minutes," Dev called to the empty room, and flicked off the row of lights above the washers. The air was warm and smelled of fabric softener and hot lint. He checked his father's watch, the one with the cracked strap that ran eight minutes slow, and added the eight in his head the way he always did. His aunt had trusted him with the keys for the first time tonight.
sections.inciting_incident: Pulling the last load of forgotten towels from dryer four, he heard something tick against the drum. He felt along the metal and closed his fingers round a ring. It was heavy and gold, with a small dark stone, and inside the band someone had engraved two names and a date.
sections.rising_action:
He held it under the light and thought about the bus pass he couldn't afford and the gas bill stuck to his aunt's fridge. The lost-property tray was right there by the till. Instead, he slid the ring into his jeans pocket. He would decide what to do with it in the morning.

But at five to ten the door banged open and a woman in a nurse's tunic hurried in, already crouching to look under the machines. "A ring," she said. "My mum's. Has anyone handed one in?" Dev felt the small weight against his leg. He told her he'd check the back room, and went to stand among the boxes of soap.

When he came out she had sat down on the bench by the window. "I'll wait," she said. "Your aunt has a camera, doesn't she? I'll ask her to check it tomorrow." She pointed at the little black dome above the dryers. Its red light had been watching him all evening.
sections.climax: Dev looked at the camera. Then at the woman. Her hands were clasped between her knees, and one thumb kept rubbing the bare place on her finger. He put his hand in his pocket. His fingers found it at once. The ring was warm now. It had taken the heat of his leg. He walked to the bench. He held it out on his open palm. He did not say where he had found it. He did not trust himself to lie, or to tell the truth.
sections.falling_action: She took it and pushed it onto her finger and pressed her other hand over it. "Thank you," she said, twice. She didn't ask anything else. At the door she turned the ring once with her thumb, as if checking it was real. The door swung shut behind her, and the bell above it rang once and was still.
sections.resolution: Dev locked the front door, then stood by the till under the big wall clock. He unbuckled his father's watch and turned the little crown until the hands matched the clock exactly. It took a while; the crown was stiff. He buckled the watch back onto his wrist and switched off the last light.

rising_beats.beat_1: He held it under the light and thought about the bus pass he couldn't afford and the gas bill stuck to his aunt's fridge. The lost-property tray was right there by the till. Instead, he slid the ring into his jeans pocket. He would decide what to do with it in the morning.
rising_beats.beat_2: But at five to ten the door banged open and a woman in a nurse's tunic hurried in, already crouching to look under the machines. "A ring," she said. "My mum's. Has anyone handed one in?" Dev felt the small weight against his leg. He told her he'd check the back room, and went to stand among the boxes of soap.
rising_beats.beat_3: When he came out she had sat down on the bench by the window. "I'll wait," she said. "Your aunt has a camera, doesn't she? I'll ask her to check it tomorrow." She pointed at the little black dome above the dryers. Its red light had been watching him all evening.

briefs.exposition: Start mid-action as Dev closes up, give the warm smell of the laundrette, and plant his father's slow watch and the trust his aunt has shown him.
briefs.inciting_incident: One discovery breaks the routine: a gold ring with an engraving, found in a dryer drum.
briefs.rising_action: Three beats that tighten the temptation: he pockets the ring, the owner's daughter arrives asking for it, then she points out the camera and settles in to wait.
briefs.climax: Slow the moment down as Dev chooses to hand the ring back, using the warmth of the ring and the woman's hands as physical detail.
briefs.falling_action: Show the woman's quiet reaction and her leaving, keeping the pace calm.
briefs.resolution: Return to the slow watch and let Dev change it, so the motif shifts meaning without anyone explaining why.

title: Last Length
picture: An indoor swimming pool with lane ropes, an empty lifeguard's high chair, and a silver whistle on a cord hanging from its arm.
character_want: To get through her final shift by the rules, without any fuss, before the pool closes for good.
character_hidden_feeling: Fear of who she is without the job, and the secret that in thirty-one years she has never swum in this pool.

sections.exposition: Rosa blew two short blasts on her whistle and pointed at the boy bombing into the shallow end. "Feet first, Kofi." Chlorine stung the back of her throat, the same as it had every evening for thirty-one years. The whistle hung on a cord she had mended so many times it was more knot than cord. Tonight the Marlowe Street Baths would close for good, and the council wanted the keys by nine.
sections.inciting_incident: At ten to nine she called the pool clear. The last few swimmers climbed out, dripping, and headed for the changing rooms. Kofi did not. He swam to the deep end, took hold of the rope, and hung there with his chin on the water. "It's the last time, miss," he said. "I'm not getting out."
sections.rising_action:
She blew the whistle. He blinked at her and didn't move. Anyone else, she would have reached for the pole. Instead, she climbed back into the high chair and checked the clock. She decided he could have five more minutes, which broke a rule she had never broken once.

But the office phone rang, and it was the man from the council, saying his team was outside and could she bring the keys to the front door now. Rosa looked at Kofi floating on his back. She decided to walk round the edge and talk him out, because shouting would only make him dig in.

Crouched at the deep end, she held out her hand. Kofi didn't take it. "My mum says you taught her to swim here," he said. "Have you ever been in? Even once?" She hadn't. Not once in thirty-one years. Headlights from the council van swept across the frosted windows.
sections.climax: Rosa stood up. She lifted the cord over her head. It caught on her ear. She set the whistle down on the starting block, and it made a small, flat sound on the tile. She stepped out of her shoes. She peeled off her socks. The tile was wet and cold under her bare feet. Kofi was watching her now, his mouth open. She sat on the edge with her legs in the water. Water slapped against the gutter. Then she pushed off.
sections.falling_action: The water closed over her shoulders, colder than she had expected. Kofi laughed out loud. They swam the length side by side, slowly, Rosa with her head held up like someone's grandmother at the seaside. At the shallow end the council man stood in the doorway, waiting.
sections.resolution: She climbed out and walked back along the side of the pool, leaving wet footprints on the tile. The whistle was still on the starting block. She looked at it for a moment. Then she picked up her shoes and left it there, a small silver thing on the edge of the empty water.

rising_beats.beat_1: She blew the whistle. He blinked at her and didn't move. Anyone else, she would have reached for the pole. Instead, she climbed back into the high chair and checked the clock. She decided he could have five more minutes, which broke a rule she had never broken once.
rising_beats.beat_2: But the office phone rang, and it was the man from the council, saying his team was outside and could she bring the keys to the front door now. Rosa looked at Kofi floating on his back. She decided to walk round the edge and talk him out, because shouting would only make him dig in.
rising_beats.beat_3: Crouched at the deep end, she held out her hand. Kofi didn't take it. "My mum says you taught her to swim here," he said. "Have you ever been in? Even once?" She hadn't. Not once in thirty-one years. Headlights from the council van swept across the frosted windows.

briefs.exposition: Open with Rosa in action, blowing the whistle, give the sting of chlorine, and plant the whistle and the fact that this is the final night.
briefs.inciting_incident: One boy refuses to leave the water at closing time on the last night.
briefs.rising_action: Three beats that squeeze Rosa between the rules and the boy: she bends a rule, the council demands the keys, then the boy asks the one question she cannot dodge.
briefs.climax: Slow down as Rosa chooses to take off the whistle and get into the pool, step by physical step.
briefs.falling_action: Show the swim itself, calmer, with the council man waiting.
briefs.resolution: Leave the whistle behind so it means something different from the opening, and end on that image.

title: The Second Cup
picture: A bus shelter on a country road at dusk, a tartan thermos flask standing on the bench beside two plastic cups.
motif: the thermos of jasmine tea and the two green cups
character_want: For her older sister's first visit home in two years to go smoothly, so that she might stay.
character_hidden_feeling: Anger that her sister left her alone with their father.

sections.exposition: Mei unscrewed the thermos, sniffed the jasmine tea, and screwed the lid back on before too much steam could escape. The bench in the bus shelter was cold through her jeans. She had brought two cups, the green ones from the back of the cupboard that nobody used anymore, and set them side by side on the bench. She checked the timetable behind the scratched plastic again. The 7:40 bus would bring Lan home for the first time in two years.
sections.inciting_incident: The 7:40 came round the bend with its windows lit, slowed, and did not stop. The driver lifted a hand as he passed. Every seat Mei could see was empty. Her phone buzzed a moment later. "Missed the connection," Lan had written. "Maybe this was a bad idea."
sections.rising_action:
Mei typed "it's fine, don't bother" and looked at it for a long time. Then she deleted it. The last bus was at nine. She wrote "there's a later one, I'll wait," pressed send before she could change her mind, and tucked the thermos inside her coat to keep it warm.

But at half past eight her dad rang from the depot, asking where she was. If he knew she was waiting for Lan, there would be shouting, the same shouting that had made Lan go. So Mei told him she was at a friend's, and promised herself she would sort it all out once Lan was here.

At nine the bus stopped, and Lan stepped down with no bag at all. She looked older and thinner. "I can only stay an hour," she said. "Then I'm getting the last bus back." She sat down on the bench and looked at Mei properly. "You're angry with me, aren't you?"
sections.climax: Mei looked at the two cups. A little steam had fogged the inside of one. She could say no. She had practised saying no all the way here. The plastic roof of the shelter ticked in the cold. A car went past and lit both their faces. Lan was not looking at the road now. She was looking at her. Mei put her hands flat on her knees. She looked at her sister's chapped knuckles. "Yes," she said. "I am."
sections.falling_action: Lan didn't argue. She nodded slowly, as if she had been waiting two years for that word. For a while neither of them spoke. A tractor rumbled along the far side of the hedge, and the noise of it faded slowly into the fields.
sections.resolution: Mei unscrewed the thermos. The tea was only warm now, not hot. She poured the first cup and held it out, and Lan took it with both hands. Then Mei poured the second, and they sat drinking side by side, the thin steam rising between them, watching the dark road, where nothing was coming yet.

rising_beats.beat_1: Mei typed "it's fine, don't bother" and looked at it for a long time. Then she deleted it. The last bus was at nine. She wrote "there's a later one, I'll wait," pressed send before she could change her mind, and tucked the thermos inside her coat to keep it warm.
rising_beats.beat_2: But at half past eight her dad rang from the depot, asking where she was. If he knew she was waiting for Lan, there would be shouting, the same shouting that had made Lan go. So Mei told him she was at a friend's, and promised herself she would sort it all out once Lan was here.
rising_beats.beat_3: At nine the bus stopped, and Lan stepped down with no bag at all. She looked older and thinner. "I can only stay an hour," she said. "Then I'm getting the last bus back." She sat down on the bench and looked at Mei properly. "You're angry with me, aren't you?"

briefs.exposition: Begin mid-action with the thermos, give the cold of the bench, and plant the two cups set out for a sister who has not arrived.
briefs.inciting_incident: One event breaks the waiting: the bus passes without Lan, and her message suggests she may not come at all.
briefs.rising_action: Three beats that build pressure on Mei's hidden anger: she chooses to keep waiting, lies to her father, then Lan arrives and asks the direct question.
briefs.climax: Slow the moment as Mei chooses to tell the truth, using the cups, the cold and her sister's hands as physical detail.
briefs.falling_action: Let Lan accept the answer quietly, with a calmer pace and the sound of the countryside.
briefs.resolution: Return to the thermos and the second cup so that the motif now means honest company, ending on an image.

title: The Spare Key
picture: A small café after closing: chairs stacked on tables, a till drawer hanging open, and a key on a frayed red ribbon hanging from a hook.
motif: the spare key on its red ribbon
character_want: To keep both her job at her uncle's café and her friendship with Leah.
character_hidden_feeling: She has known for weeks that Leah's family is struggling and has said nothing.

sections.exposition: Amira flipped the last chair onto its table and wiped the burnt-milk smell off her hands with a tea towel. On the hook beside the till hung the spare key on its red ribbon, the one she and Leah took turns using for the early shift. Leah had tied the ribbon on in September, the week they both started. The radio was still murmuring the late news. Uncle Sami was counting the till drawer for the third time.
sections.inciting_incident: "Forty pounds short," he said. "Again." He turned his phone towards her. On the screen, grainy and green, a hand slid into the open drawer at closing time on Tuesday. On the wrist was a silver bracelet with a tiny charm shaped like a moon. "Whose bracelet is that?"
sections.rising_action:
Amira knew it the moment she saw the moon. She said the picture was too blurry to tell. While her uncle went to the back to fetch the cash bag, she decided to message Leah first, so that Leah could explain before anyone said her name out loud.

But Leah's answer came back in seconds. "please don't tell him. i'll pay it back. it was for mum's electric." Amira read it twice. So she took her own wages envelope out of her bag and decided she'd slip forty pounds into the drawer and let the whole thing disappear.

Before she could reach the till, Uncle Sami came back and locked the drawer. "I'm phoning the police in the morning," he said. "The insurance won't pay without a report. They'll take this film and find the bracelet themselves." He leaned on the counter. "Unless you tell me first."
sections.climax: Amira looked at the hook. The red ribbon had frayed at one end where Leah kept twisting it. Her wages envelope was still in her hand. The paper had gone soft in her grip. She put it on the counter. She pushed it across to him. "It was Leah," she said. "Her mum can't pay the electric. That's the forty. Please don't phone anyone." Her uncle didn't move. The coffee machine hissed behind him. Then she stood still and waited.
sections.falling_action: Uncle Sami looked at the envelope for a long time without touching it. His face looked tired, not angry. Then he slid it back across the counter towards her. He said he would talk to Leah himself, tomorrow, before her shift, and that nobody was phoning anybody. He switched off the coffee machine.
sections.resolution: On her way out, Amira took the spare key down from its hook. She held it for a moment, the ribbon soft and grubby between her fingers. Then she untied the frayed end, pulled it straight, retied it in a tight double knot, and hung the key back where Leah would find it in the morning.

rising_beats.beat_1: Amira knew it the moment she saw the moon. She said the picture was too blurry to tell. While her uncle went to the back to fetch the cash bag, she decided to message Leah first, so that Leah could explain before anyone said her name out loud.
rising_beats.beat_2: But Leah's answer came back in seconds. "please don't tell him. i'll pay it back. it was for mum's electric." Amira read it twice. So she took her own wages envelope out of her bag and decided she'd slip forty pounds into the drawer and let the whole thing disappear.
rising_beats.beat_3: Before she could reach the till, Uncle Sami came back and locked the drawer. "I'm phoning the police in the morning," he said. "The insurance won't pay without a report. They'll take this film and find the bracelet themselves." He leaned on the counter. "Unless you tell me first."

briefs.exposition: Open mid-task as Amira closes the café, give the burnt-milk smell, and plant the shared spare key on its red ribbon.
briefs.inciting_incident: One event: her uncle shows her footage of a hand in the till wearing a bracelet she recognises.
briefs.rising_action: Three beats that trap Amira between family and friend: she stalls and messages Leah, tries to cover the money herself, then her uncle closes that exit by threatening the police.
briefs.climax: Slow down as Amira chooses to tell the truth and offer her own wages, with physical detail of the ribbon and envelope.
briefs.falling_action: Show the uncle's quiet, unexpected response, at a calmer pace.
briefs.resolution: Return to the key and ribbon so they now stand for a repaired friendship, ending on her action.

title: One Line in Yellow
picture: An empty school science lab after hours, a printer in the corner with warm pages in its tray, and a yellow highlighter lying on an open revision guide.
character_want: To pass his chemistry mock so he can keep his place at the football academy.
character_hidden_feeling: A private belief that he is stupid.

sections.exposition: Ollie dragged the yellow highlighter across another line of his revision guide until the whole page glowed the same flat colour. Every sentence looked important, so he marked all of them. The lab smelled of gas taps and old rubber tubing, and the radiator under the window clanked. Ms Okoye had let him stay after school to revise, as long as he left by five. His place at the football academy depended on a pass.
sections.inciting_incident: At ten to five the printer in the corner whirred, coughed, and pushed out a stack of warm pages. Ollie went over to switch it off. The top sheet said, in bold capitals, "Year 11 Chemistry Mock Examination, Paper 2. Confidential." The mock was in two days.
sections.rising_action:
He turned the stack face down at once, as if someone might be standing behind him. Nobody was. The first question was already in his head anyway, something about rates of reaction. He decided to leave the papers in the tray, pack his bag, and go before he saw anything else.

But the lab door wouldn't open. The caretaker had locked the corridor early, and the handle only rattled. Ollie tried the fire door, which was chained. So he rang Ms Okoye's number from the card on her desk and told her he was stuck, and that her printer had been doing things on its own.

"I'm ten minutes away," she said. "Don't touch anything." She hung up before he could explain. Ten minutes. The papers sat in the tray, a hand's width from his elbow. The room was silent except for the radiator, and nobody would ever know what he did with ten minutes alone.
sections.climax: Ollie took an envelope from the box on her desk. He picked up the stack, still face down. The paper was warm. He kept his eyes on the ceiling tiles while he slid it in. One page bent. The radiator clanked twice. He licked the flap. It tasted of glue. He pressed it shut with the side of his fist. Then he wrote across the front in capital letters: "DIDN'T READ IT. OLLIE." He set it on her chair.
sections.falling_action: Ms Okoye unlocked the door eight minutes later, still in her coat. She picked up the envelope, read the front, and looked at him over her glasses. She didn't open it. "Thank you, Oliver," she said, and went to find the caretaker, leaving the door propped open.
sections.resolution: Ollie sat back down at the bench. He turned to a clean page in the revision guide, the one on rates of reaction, and read it slowly from the top. Halfway down he stopped, uncapped the highlighter, and drew one yellow line under one sentence. Out in the corridor the caretaker's keys jingled past. Ollie read on.

rising_beats.beat_1: He turned the stack face down at once, as if someone might be standing behind him. Nobody was. The first question was already in his head anyway, something about rates of reaction. He decided to leave the papers in the tray, pack his bag, and go before he saw anything else.

So he rang Ms Okoye's number from the card on her desk and told her he was stuck, and that her printer had been doing things on its own.
rising_beats.beat_3: "I'm ten minutes away," she said. "Don't touch anything." She hung up before he could explain. Ten minutes. The papers sat in the tray, a hand's width from his elbow. The room was silent except for the radiator, and nobody would ever know what he did with ten minutes alone.

briefs.exposition: Start mid-action with the highlighter, give the smell and sound of the lab, and plant the habit of marking every line.
briefs.inciting_incident: One discovery: the confidential mock paper prints out in front of him.
briefs.rising_action: Three beats that remove every way out: he tries to leave, finds himself locked in, then is left alone with the paper for ten minutes.
briefs.climax: Slow down as Ollie chooses to seal the paper away unread, using precise physical actions with the envelope.
briefs.falling_action: Show the teacher's calm reaction, without a speech.
briefs.resolution: Return to the highlighter so that one line, not every line, is marked; end on the small action of reading on.

title: Stars on the Ceiling
picture: A bare bedroom full of taped cardboard boxes, with pale plastic glow-in-the-dark stars stuck to the ceiling.
motif: the glow-in-the-dark stars on the ceiling
character_want: To finish packing on the last night in the house and keep her younger brother calm.
character_hidden_feeling: She is relieved to be leaving, and ashamed of being relieved.

sections.exposition: "Hold the chair still," Lena said, and stretched up to pick at the first plastic star on the ceiling. Max held the chair with both hands. The room smelled of packing tape and the dust from behind the radiator. Their dad had stuck the stars up when Max was born, forty of them in shapes that weren't real constellations, and in the dark they still glowed a weak green.
sections.inciting_incident: The star came away with a little tearing sound, and a crumb of plaster fell into Lena's eye. Max let go of the chair. "Stop," he said. "Leave them. They're for the next kid." He climbed onto his bed, fully dressed, and pulled the duvet over his head.
sections.rising_action:
Lena stood on the chair, rubbing her eye, holding one green star. Arguing with him would take all night. She decided she would wait until he was asleep and take the rest down quietly, so that he would only see a blank ceiling when it was too late to mind.

But when she climbed back up at eleven, Max's voice came from under the duvet. "Are you sad we're going?" Lena kept her arm up. She said yes, of course she was, because that was what he needed to hear. Then she chose to keep peeling, faster, star after star.

Their mum called up the stairs that the removal van was coming at six, not nine, and the lights had to go off now. Max sat up. He had been watching her the whole time. "You don't look sad," he said. "You want to go, don't you?" Downstairs, the light switch clicked.
sections.climax: In the dark the stars came on, the twelve she had left. Lena stood on the chair. One star was still stuck to her thumb. She could feel its points. She could say no again. Max was waiting. The duvet rustled. Downstairs a box scraped across the floor. She climbed down. She sat on the end of his bed, and the mattress dipped. "Yes," she said. "I want to go. I'm sorry." She kept her eyes on the green shapes above them.
sections.falling_action: Max was quiet for a long time. Then he said that he wanted to go a bit too, sometimes, when the shouting started, and that he hadn't told anyone. Outside, a car door slammed and someone laughed in the street. He lay back down. Lena lay beside him on top of the duvet, still in her trainers.
sections.resolution: Before the van came, Lena peeled the last star from her thumb and pressed it onto the inside lid of Max's box of books, where nobody but him would see it. She smoothed it down with her fingertip. Then she taped the box shut and wrote his name across the top in thick black letters.

rising_beats.beat_1: Lena stood on the chair, rubbing her eye, holding one green star. Arguing with him would take all night. She decided she would wait until he was asleep and take the rest down quietly, so that he would only see a blank ceiling when it was too late to mind.
rising_beats.beat_2: But when she climbed back up at eleven, Max's voice came from under the duvet. "Are you sad we're going?" Lena kept her arm up. She said yes, of course she was, because that was what he needed to hear. Then she chose to keep peeling, faster, star after star.

briefs.exposition: Open with dialogue mid-task, give the smell of packing, and plant the stars their father stuck up.
briefs.inciting_incident: One event: Max refuses to let her take the stars down.
briefs.rising_action: Three beats that corner Lena's hidden relief: she plans to wait him out, lies that she is sad, then he asks her straight out as the lights go off.
briefs.climax: Slow down as Lena chooses to tell Max the truth, with the star on her thumb and the dipping mattress as physical detail.
briefs.falling_action: Let Max answer with his own small confession, at a calmer pace.
briefs.resolution: Give the last star a new place and meaning, ending on the action of taping and labelling his box.

title: The Barrier
picture: An ice rink under bright lights, a small child in a red helmet alone in the middle of the ice, and a teenager's wrist with a frayed white lace tied round it resting on the barrier.
motif: the frayed white skate lace round her wrist
character_want: To drop her little cousin at a skating class and leave the rink before anyone recognises her.
character_hidden_feeling: She still misses skating, and is ashamed that she quit after a fall here four years ago.

sections.exposition: Nadia yanked the laces of Bea's rental skates tight and tied a double bow. "Too tight," Bea said. "Good," said Nadia. The rink smelled the way it always had, of cold metal and chips from the café upstairs, and the hum of the freezers came up through the rubber floor. Round her wrist she still wore a frayed white lace from her old competition boots. She had not been back in four years.
sections.inciting_incident: A woman with a clipboard came out of the office and announced that the coach was ill. The beginners' class would only run if a grown-up skated with each child. The other parents shook their heads and started zipping up coats. Bea looked up at Nadia with her helmet tipped over one eye.
sections.rising_action:
Nadia said no before Bea could ask. She told her they would come back next week, and decided they would leave now, before anyone at the desk looked at her name on the booking. She started gathering Bea's shoes from under the bench. Nobody needed to know who she was.

But when she turned round with the shoes, Bea had already stepped through the open gate and was sliding, arms out, towards the middle. Nadia ran to the barrier in her trainers. She would hire skates and stay at the edge, she decided, holding the barrier and calling Bea back to her.

By the time she had laced the hired boots, Bea had fallen flat in the centre of the rink, where the ice was scratched and grey. She was crying, much too far away to reach. The woman with the clipboard had gone back into the office. There was nobody else on the ice at all.
sections.climax: Nadia stood at the gate. Her hands were on the barrier. The plastic was cold and sticky with old drink. Bea's crying echoed off the roof. Nadia looked down at her own feet. The hired blades were dull. Cold air rose off the ice. A tannoy crackled and went quiet. She took one hand off the barrier. Then the other. She pushed. The first stroke wobbled. The second didn't. She bent her knees, the way she had been taught at six.
sections.falling_action: She reached Bea in six strokes and scooped her up under the arms. Bea stopped crying almost at once, more surprised than hurt. Nadia set her on her feet and held both her mittens, and they glided back towards the gate together, slowly.
sections.resolution: At the bench, Nadia untied the frayed lace from her wrist. She threaded it through the top hooks of Bea's rental skate, where the old lace had snapped, and pulled it tight. It was too long, so she wrapped it twice round the ankle. "Too tight," Bea said. Nadia tied a double bow and led her back onto the ice.

She would hire skates and stay at the edge, she decided, holding the barrier and calling Bea back to her.
rising_beats.beat_3: By the time she had laced the hired boots, Bea had fallen flat in the centre of the rink, where the ice was scratched and grey. She was crying, much too far away to reach. The woman with the clipboard had gone back into the office. There was nobody else on the ice at all.

briefs.exposition: Open mid-action with dialogue as Nadia laces Bea's skates, give the smell and hum of the rink, and plant the old lace on her wrist.
briefs.inciting_incident: One event: the coach is ill and the class will only run if an adult skates.
briefs.rising_action: Three beats that pull Nadia back onto the ice: she tries to leave, Bea goes out alone, then Bea falls where the barrier cannot reach.
briefs.climax: Slow down as Nadia chooses to let go of the barrier, one hand at a time, one stroke at a time.
briefs.falling_action: Show the rescue as calm and simple, without commentary.
briefs.resolution: Use the lace to keep Bea skating, so the motif turns from a souvenir of quitting into something useful; end on an action.

title: Arrivals
picture: An airport arrivals hall, people leaning on a metal rail, and an older woman holding a hand-lettered cardboard sign.
motif: the hand-lettered cardboard sign reading KIT
character_want: To meet her grandson for the first time and have him like her.
character_hidden_feeling: Shame that she cut off her daughter, his mother, nineteen years ago.

sections.exposition: Esther went over the letters on the cardboard sign a second time, pressing hard with the marker until the K was thick and black. Her good coat was buttoned to the top. The arrivals hall smelled of coffee and floor polish, and the metal rail was cold under her forearms. KIT, the sign said. She had written it three times that morning before she was happy. His flight from Toronto had landed twenty minutes ago.
sections.inciting_incident: Her phone buzzed against her hip. It was her daughter, the first message in nineteen years. "He doesn't know why we never visited," it said. "He thinks you were ill. Tell him or don't. Up to you." The doors slid open and passengers poured through, pushing trolleys.
sections.rising_action:
Esther turned the phone face down on the rail. He would never need to know. She decided she would be the kind, ill grandmother he expected, and lifted the sign higher, so that he would see it first and not have time to see anything else in her face.

But the young man who stopped in front of her had her daughter's eyebrows and a rucksack, and he was smiling. "Gran?" he said. "Mum said you'd tell me what happened. She said I should ask." Esther lowered the sign. She suggested a coffee first, at the café by the exit, to buy herself ten minutes.

Kit shook his head and showed her his phone. His connecting train left in twenty-five minutes, and the next one wasn't until tomorrow. "We can just talk here," he said, and leaned on the rail beside her. People flowed round them with their suitcases. There was nowhere else to go.
sections.climax: Esther looked at the sign in her hands. The card had gone soft at the corner where she had gripped it. Her thumb had smudged the I. She thought of the word ill. She could say it. A trolley wheel squeaked past behind her. He would believe her. She folded the sign once. Then she held it flat against her coat. "I wasn't ill," she said. "Your mother was pregnant with you. I told her not to come home."
sections.falling_action: Kit didn't move away. He looked at her for a while, then at the departures board, then back. "Okay," he said quietly. "She told me you'd say that, if you said anything." A family nearby was cheering someone through the doors. He didn't smile, but he didn't leave either. Above them, the board flicked over.
sections.resolution: When his train was called, Esther held out the folded sign. Kit took it and opened it and looked at his own name in her thick black letters. He slid it into the side pocket of his rucksack, with the top edge sticking out. Then he picked up his bag and walked towards the platform.

She said I should ask." Esther lowered the sign. She suggested a coffee first, at the café by the exit, to buy herself ten minutes.
rising_beats.beat_3: Kit shook his head and showed her his phone. His connecting train left in twenty-five minutes, and the next one wasn't until tomorrow. "We can just talk here," he said, and leaned on the rail beside her. People flowed round them with their suitcases. There was nowhere else to go.

briefs.exposition: Open mid-action as Esther inks the sign, give the smell of the hall and the cold rail, and plant the sign with Kit's name.
briefs.inciting_incident: One event: her daughter's first message in nineteen years gives Esther a lie she could tell.
briefs.rising_action: Three beats that close in on Esther's shame: she plans to keep the lie, Kit asks directly, then he has no time for a delay.
briefs.climax: Slow down as Esther chooses to tell the truth, using the soft card and the smudged letter as physical detail.
briefs.falling_action: Show Kit's restrained reaction, calm and unresolved.
briefs.resolution: Let Kit keep the sign so it now carries the truth between them, ending on him walking away.

title: The Armband
picture: A muddy football pitch under floodlights at dusk, the penalty spot gleaming, and a captain's armband lying on a kit bag by the touchline.
character_want: To win the cup final for her team.
character_hidden_feeling: She still blames her best friend Jess, a little, for missing the deciding penalty last year.

sections.exposition: Zara pulled the captain's armband up over her elbow for the fourth time, and for the fourth time it slid back down to her wrist. The floodlights buzzed, and the mud round the penalty spot shone like wet chocolate. Last year Jess had worn this armband, in this final, against this team. One-all at full time. The referee walked over with a pen and a blank card.
sections.inciting_incident: "Your coach has been sent to the stand," the referee said. "The captain picks the five takers. Write them down in order." She handed Zara the card. Before Zara had even uncapped the pen, Jess was beside her, hands on her knees, breathing hard. "Put me fifth," Jess said. "Please. I need this one."
sections.rising_action:
Zara wrote four names without stopping. The fifth line stayed empty. Priya, who had only joined in January, had scored every penalty in training; Jess had not taken one since last year. So Zara chose to leave the space blank for now, and asked the referee for a minute with her team.

But the team had heard Jess, and they stood in a loose circle, looking at Zara. Nobody said Priya's name. Jess had been their captain and their friend for three seasons. Zara decided she would let the shootout settle it: if they were still level after four, she would think again.

"Card," said the referee, holding out her hand. "Now, or your team forfeits." The other captain had already handed hers in. Zara looked at the blank fifth line, at Jess's mud-streaked face, at Priya standing quietly at the back. There was no time left to wait for anything at all.
sections.climax: Zara put the card against her thigh. The pen was cold. Mud had dried in a crust on her knuckles. The ink skipped, and the first letter came out crooked. P. She went over it again. She wrote the rest slowly. Priya. Her studs sank a little into the soft ground. She capped the pen. She handed the card over. Then she turned to Jess, because Jess deserved to hear it from her face. "Priya's fifth," she said. "I'm sorry."
sections.falling_action: Jess stared at her. Then she nodded once and walked to the halfway line with the others, and she didn't look back. When Priya's penalty hit the net, the team ran in a wild knot towards the goal. Jess was the last to reach them.
sections.resolution: Later, when the pitch had emptied, Zara found Jess sitting on her kit bag by the touchline. She slid the armband off, rolled it up, and held it out. Jess didn't take it. Zara set it down on the bag beside her anyway, then sat on the cold grass next to her, and waited. Across the pitch, the floodlights went off one bank at a time.

Priya, who had only joined in January, had scored every penalty in training; Jess had not taken one since last year. So Zara chose to leave the space blank for now, and asked the referee for a minute with her team.

briefs.exposition: Open mid-action with the loose armband, give the buzz of the floodlights and the mud, and plant the armband's history with Jess.
briefs.inciting_incident: One event: the coach is sent off and Zara must choose the penalty takers as Jess begs to go fifth.
briefs.rising_action: Three beats that squeeze Zara between friend and team: she leaves the line blank, the team's silence pushes her to delay, then the referee removes all time.
briefs.climax: Slow down as Zara chooses Priya and tells Jess to her face, using the pen, the card and the crooked letter as physical detail.
briefs.falling_action: Show the consequence: Jess's silence and the winning penalty, kept brief and calm.
briefs.resolution: Return to the armband as an offer to Jess that is not yet accepted; end on the image of Zara waiting.

title: Bowline
picture: The open deck of a small car ferry on grey water, a thick coil of rope on the wet steel, and an island low on the horizon.
character_want: To cross to the island for his sister's wedding without having to speak to anyone from his old life.
character_hidden_feeling: He left the island four years ago without saying goodbye to his best friend Callum.

sections.exposition: Ewan tied and untied a bowline in the end of his bootlace while the ferry pulled away from the slipway, the way he used to in maths lessons when he was bored. Diesel fumes drifted across the car deck, mixed with the cold salt off the water. The island was a grey hump on the horizon. He was home for his sister's wedding, and he planned to stay in the car the whole way.
sections.inciting_incident: Someone knocked on his window. A deckhand in an orange jacket was bending down, pointing at the parking line, and Ewan knew him before the glass was halfway down. Callum. Broader now, with a beard, but the same chipped front tooth. Callum's face went still. "Ewan," he said. "You're back, then."
sections.rising_action:
Ewan said hi and nothing else, and wound the window back up. Callum stood there a second longer, then walked off down the line of cars. Ewan decided he would keep his head down and his eyes on his phone, and get off at the other end without saying anything at all.

But halfway across the swell got up, and the tannoy told all passengers to leave the car deck and go up to the lounge. Callum was behind the little counter, pouring tea. Ewan chose a seat by the window, as far from him as he could get, and planned to talk only about the weather.

The ferry gave a heavy lurch, and on the open deck a mooring line slid loose, snaking across the wet steel. "Need a hand out here," Callum shouted through the door. "Now." There was nobody else in the lounge but an old woman asleep. Ewan was the only one who could go.
sections.climax: The rope was soaked and heavy. Ewan took the end. Callum took the middle. Spray hit the side of his face. They hauled together, and the line came in across the deck in long wet loops. Callum held the end out to him without a word. Ewan looked at it. His fingers knew the knot. Rabbit out of the hole. Round the tree. Back down the hole. He pulled it tight. "I should have told you I was going," he said.
sections.falling_action: Callum checked the knot, tugging it once. It held. He didn't answer straight away. He coiled the rest of the line on the deck in neat rings, then sat back on his heels, wiping his hands on his jacket. "You should have," he said at last. "Aye."
sections.resolution: When the ferry bumped against the island slipway, Callum threw the line to the man on the pier. Ewan watched the bowline drop over the bollard and pull tight as the boat swung in. Then he went down to his car, and left the window open as he drove off the ramp.

Ewan chose a seat by the window, as far from him as he could get, and planned to talk only about the weather.

briefs.exposition: Open mid-action with Ewan tying a bowline, give the diesel and salt air, and plant his plan to hide in the car.
briefs.inciting_incident: One event: the deckhand knocking on his window is Callum, the friend he left without a word.
briefs.rising_action: Three beats that force Ewan out of hiding: he shuts the window, is sent up to the lounge, then a loose line leaves only him to help.
briefs.climax: Slow down as Ewan ties the knot Callum hands him and chooses to apologise, using the rope's weight and the rhyme for the knot.
briefs.falling_action: Show Callum's slow, plain reply, calmer in pace.
briefs.resolution: Bring the bowline back holding the ferry to the island, and end on the small action of the open window.

title: The Recipe Card
picture: A small bakery kitchen at dawn, trays of glazed buns cooling, and a stained handwritten recipe card pinned above the oven in a cloudy plastic sleeve.
motif: the stained recipe card above the oven
character_want: To run her grandmother's bakery alone on a Saturday and make the famous buns exactly right.
character_hidden_feeling: She has never felt as good as her grandmother at anything.

sections.exposition: Ana slapped the dough onto the floured bench and pushed the heel of her hand into it, again and again, the way Grandma Lidia did. The kitchen was already warm from the ovens and smelled of yeast and orange peel. Above the oven, in a cloudy plastic sleeve, hung the recipe card for the famous Saturday buns, stained with forty years of butter. Ana had read it so often she could recite it.
sections.inciting_incident: Reaching into the back of the storeroom for a fresh sack of flour, she knocked over a cardboard box. Twelve packets slid out across the floor. "Bake-Rite Sweet Bun Mix," they said, in cheerful red letters. On the side of each one was a recipe. It matched the card exactly.
sections.rising_action:
Ana sat down on a sack of sugar and laughed, though it didn't feel funny. Forty years. She shoved the packets back into the box and pushed it behind the mop bucket. She decided she would make the buns properly instead, from scratch, the way everyone believed they had always been made.

But her scratch buns came out of the oven flat and pale, and the market queue started at seven. It was twenty to. Ana looked at the mop bucket for a long moment. So she tore open two packets, telling herself this was the only way to have trays on the counter by seven, and that nobody would ever know.

At ten to seven the bell rang. A man from the local paper stood in the doorway with a camera on his shoulder. "Your gran said I could film the secret recipe," he said, and held up his phone. Grandma Lidia's voice came out of it, bright and loud: "Show him the card, love."
sections.climax: Ana looked at the card above the oven. Then at the camera's red light. Her hands were still dusty with mix. Flour dust hung in the light. She wiped them on her apron, slowly, one finger at a time. She walked to the storeroom. The box was behind the bucket where she had left it. She carried it out and set it on the counter. She took out one packet. She turned it to face the lens.
sections.falling_action: For a second nobody said anything. Then her grandmother's laugh crackled out of the phone, loud and helpless. "Forty years," she said, "and nobody ever looked in the storeroom." The man from the paper was laughing too, still filming, as the first customer pushed the door open.
sections.resolution: That evening, Ana took the card down from above the oven and slid it out of its sleeve. On the blank back she wrote her own recipe, the flat one, with her corrections squeezed into the margin. Then she slid the card back into its sleeve and pinned it up with her side facing out.

briefs.exposition: Open mid-action with Ana kneading, give the warm smell of yeast and orange peel, and plant the famous recipe card.
briefs.inciting_incident: One discovery: the secret recipe is a supermarket packet mix hidden in the storeroom.
briefs.rising_action: Three beats that build pressure on Ana's fear of not measuring up: she tries from scratch, fails and secretly uses the mix, then a camera arrives to film the recipe.
briefs.climax: Slow down as Ana chooses to show the packet to the camera, with her dusty hands and each deliberate step as physical detail.
briefs.falling_action: Let the grandmother's laughter answer the choice, calmly and briefly.
briefs.resolution: Return to the recipe card, now carrying Ana's own recipe on the back; end on the image of her side facing out.
